e-562.knowledge_point: Finding the Velocity of a Particle Whose Acceleration Is Given By a Polynomial
e-562.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\textrm m / \textrm s^2,$ given by the function $a(t) = 4t^2 - 3t^3,$ where $t$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=2\,\textrm m / \textrm s$ when $t=0 \,\textrm s,$ calculate the velocity (in $\textrm m / \textrm s$) of the particle at time $t.$
e-562.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (4{t}^{2}-3{t}^{3})\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{4}{3}{t}^{3}-\frac{3}{4}{t}^{4}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0) = 2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =\frac{4}{3}(0)^{3}-\frac{3}{4}(0)^{4}+C \\ C & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t) = \dfrac{4}{3}t^3 -\dfrac{3}{4}t^4 + 2.$

e-563.knowledge_point: Finding the Velocity of a Particle Whose Acceleration Is Not a Polynomial
e-563.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\textrm m / \textrm s^2,$ given by the function $a(t) =2e^{-t}+6t^2$, where $t$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=-4 \,\textrm m / \textrm s$ when $t=0 \,\textrm s,$ calculate the speed of the particle at the moment  $t=1\,\textrm{s}.$
e-563.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (2{e}^{-t}+6{t}^{2})\text{d}t \\  & =2(-{e}^{-t})+\frac{6}{3}{t}^{3}+C \\  & =-2{e}^{-t}+2{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(0) = -4.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-4 & =-2{e}^{-0}+2\cdot {0}^{3}+C \\ -4 & =-2+0+C \\ C & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t) = -2  e^{-t}+ 2t^3 -2.$

We evaluate the velocity at time $t=1\,\textrm{s}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =-2{e}^{-1}+2(1)^{3}-2 \\  & =-2{e}^{-1}+2-2 \\  & =-\frac{2}{e}\,\text{m/s}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the speed is equal to $|v(t)|,$ we conclude that the speed of the particle is $\dfrac 2 e\,\textrm{m/s}.$

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration, measured in m/s2, given by the function a(t)=6t2−2t−10, where t is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity v=−4m/s when t=1s, calculate the speed of the particle at the moment t=3s.

a
24m/s
b
15m/s
c
16m/s
d
22m/s
e
20m/s
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating gives v(t)=2t^3-t^2-10t+C. Using v(1)=-4 gives -9+C=-4, so C=5. Therefore v(3)=54-9-30+5=20 m/s, and the speed is |v(3)|=20 m/s.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=6{t}^{2}-2t-10$, where $t$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=-4\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=1\,\text{s}$, calculate the speed of the particle at the moment $t=3\,\text{s}.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (6{t}^{2}-2t-10)\text{d}t \\  & =2{t}^{3}-{t}^{2}-10t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1)=-4.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-4 & =2(1)^{3}-(1)^{2}-10(1)+C \\ -4 & =2-1-10+C \\ C & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=2{t}^{3}-{t}^{2}-10t+5.$

We evaluate the velocity at time $t=3\,\text{s}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(3) & =2(3)^{3}-(3)^{2}-10(3)+5 \\  & =54-9-30+5 \\  & =20\,\text{m/s}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the speed is equal to $|v(t)|,$ we conclude that the speed of the particle is $20\,\text{m/s}.$

content.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (-6{e}^{-2t})\,\text{d}t \\  & =-6(-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-2t})+C \\  & =3{e}^{-2t}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(0)=2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =3{e}^{0}+C \\ 2 & =3+C \\ C & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=3{e}^{-2t}-1.$

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration, measured in m/s2, given by the function a(t)=1(t+1)2, where t is the time in seconds. If the particle has a velocity v=1 when t=0s, find the velocity (in m/s) of the particle at time t.

a
v(t)=−1t+1+1
b
v(t)=−1t+1+2
c
v(t)=2t+1
d
v(t)=1t+1
e
v(t)=−1t+1−2
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating a(t)=(t+1)^{-2} gives v(t)=-1/(t+1)+C. Since v(0)=1, -1+C=1, so C=2. Thus v(t)=-1/(t+1)+2.

after.name: Question 8
after.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=\frac{1}{(t+1)^{2}}$, where $t$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has a velocity $v=1$ when $t=0\,\text{s}$, find the velocity (in $\text{m/s}$)  of the particle at time $t.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \frac{1}{(t+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{1}{t+1}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(0)=1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =-\frac{1}{0+1}+C \\ 1 & =-1+C \\ C & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=-\frac{1}{t+1}+2.$

content.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=\frac{1}{(t+1)^{2}}$, where $t$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has a velocity $v=1$ when $t=0\,\text{s}$, find the velocity (in $\text{m/s}$)  of the particle at time $t.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \frac{1}{(t+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{1}{t+1}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(0)=1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =-\frac{1}{0+1}+C \\ 1 & =-1+C \\ C & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=-\frac{1}{t+1}+2.$
